history.title: Selection Week

data.body:
**Due:** (your teacher will tell you)

Most people can define natural selection and still explain it wrongly. This unit spends as much time on the wrong version as the right one, because the wrong version is the one that survives.

1. Read **How Populations Change**. Mark every sentence that says what selection does *not* do.
2. Learn the words in **Selection Vocabulary**, then win the **Matching** game and the **Memory** game.
3. Work through **The Selection Model** to see why the argument holds together.
4. Study the **Right Version, Wrong Version** chart.
5. Sort the cards in **How It Works or How It Doesn't?** — several are close.
6. Fill in **Selection Notes** as you read.
7. Take **Selection Check**.
8. Lock it in with **Remember the Selection Model**.
9. Read **Questions People Ask About Evolution**.
10. Finish with **Investigation: Track the Trait**.

Bring one example of an organism that seems perfectly built for where it lives. 🧬

Picture panels: Variation and inheritance; Population change and fitness; Habitat context; Mutation and resistance. Text-free illustrations use editable captions and image-specific descriptions. Diagrams simplify scale, anatomy and processes; colors and tokens are explained in captions. Follow the lesson text for scientific context. Educator review is pending.

history.title: How Populations Change
history.data:
## How Populations Change

Beetles in one habitat can have different colors. Suppose these differences are inherited and affect how many offspring they leave. Over many **generations**, the share of each color in the **population** can change. This can be evolution by natural **selection**.

Individuals can grow, learn and adjust during life. These **acquired** changes do not, by themselves, show that a population has evolved. We need to track inherited differences across generations.

### Follow the process

**Variation** means that individuals differ. A useful variant may already be present when conditions change. New variants can also arise later through mutation or arrive with new members. Need does not direct a useful **mutation**, which is a change in DNA.

A **heritable** trait can pass from parent to offspring through genes. Many traits also depend on the surroundings. Building muscles through training does not automatically copy those muscles into a child's DNA.

The **environment** affects which traits help. Food, predators and mates all matter. Crowding is not required for selection. A trait might change success in finding a mate or the number of offspring produced.

**Fitness** means success in passing genes to later generations, compared with others in that setting. Survival matters when it affects reproduction. Fitness does not mean strength, health or personal worth.

A helpful inherited trait can become more common. Its **frequency** is how common it is. But this is not guaranteed. Chance can remove even a helpful variant. Changes due to chance are called genetic drift. Drift can occur in any population and often has stronger effects in small ones.

### Read the pictures as models

Our rows of eight beetles have two, then four, then six dark beetles. These are invented counts. They show new generations, not the same beetles changing color. A moth picture shows how a background can affect visibility. It cannot prove selection by itself. We also need evidence about inheritance and offspring.

The bacteria panel is a simple counter model. Assume two bacteria already have inherited **resistance** to one antibiotic. They survive exposure and reproduce. Their descendants can make resistance more common. In real cases, new mutations and genes passed between microbes can also matter. A survivor alone is not proof of resistance. We use counters, not live bacteria or drugs.

### No planned goal

A mutation can be harmful, helpful or have little effect in a given setting. A population may never gain a trait it needs. Natural selection has no plan for a perfect organism.

An **adaptation** is an inherited trait shaped by past selection. It may help in one setting and be a drawback in another. Ask what varied, what was inherited, and how success in reproduction differed. Then consider chance and other possible causes.

data.instructions: Two cards carry what you will use on every example. Read the given one, build your own, then explain why yours works.
data.sourceExcerpt: Inherited variation and differences in reproductive contribution can change frequencies across generations. Individuals also grow and learn; these lifetime changes alone are not population evolution.

cards.target: Four questions for a selection explanation
essentialFacts: What variation is available? New variants can also arise or arrive later.
How do variants differ in reproductive contribution?
cards.aiExample: Ask four questions: What differs? What is inherited? What are the conditions? Who leaves more offspring? Then count the traits in later generations.
cards.mapping: The questions connect parts of an explanation. They are not a fixed order. Include chance as another possible cause.

history.title: Selection Check

questions.question: Which observation describes population evolution that natural selection could help explain?
options: The proportion carrying a heritable trait changes across generations
Each individual gradually adjusts its own body over its lifetime
Every member of the species develops the useful trait at once
The environment changes to suit the species living in it
questions.correctAnswer: The proportion carrying a heritable trait changes across generations

questions.question: Which statement about variation available to selection is accurate?
options: New needs direct the production of a matching inherited trait
Variants can exist already or arise later, without direction by need
Useful variants appear only after every older variant has vanished
The environment gives parents the exact DNA changes they need
questions.correctAnswer: Variants can exist already or arise later, without direction by need

questions.question: A weightlifter builds a great deal of muscle. What do their children inherit?
options: The exact muscle gains, because the parent trained hard
Part of the gained muscle, but only in the first generation
Not an automatic DNA copy of the muscle gained by training
The gained muscle itself, but no ability to maintain it
questions.correctAnswer: Not an automatic DNA copy of the muscle gained by training

questions.question: A few bacteria survive a course of antibiotics. What does this show?
options: The drug toughened those particular bacteria up
Those bacteria learned to withstand the drug over time
The drug caused a helpful mutation in the survivors
Survival alone does not establish inherited resistance or when it arose
questions.correctAnswer: Survival alone does not establish inherited resistance or when it arose

questions.question: In biology, what does fitness mean?
options: Leaving more surviving offspring in this environment
Being the strongest member of the population
Being physically healthy and free of disease
Being able to survive in the widest range of places
questions.correctAnswer: Leaving more surviving offspring in this environment

questions.question: Why does natural selection have no planned destination?
options: Because it works far too slowly to have any pattern
Because what counts as helpful depends on current conditions
Because mutations occur at a completely steady rate
Because every trait is equally useful in every environment
questions.correctAnswer: Because what counts as helpful depends on current conditions

questions.question: Which statement about mutation is accurate?
options: It helps the organism because every change is an improvement
It always harms the organism because every change breaks a gene
It can help, harm or have little effect, depending on the setting
It is made on purpose when an organism needs a particular trait
questions.correctAnswer: It can help, harm or have little effect, depending on the setting

questions.question: Rewrite this sentence so it is accurate: "Over time, the moths turned darker so they could hide against the sooty trees."
questions.expectedAnswer: In this model, dark and pale variants have a heritable basis. Darker moths may be less visible on dark bark and leave more offspring. Their frequency can then rise across generations. This requires evidence of inheritance and reproductive differences; a picture alone is insufficient. It does not mean individuals changed color because they needed camouflage.

questions.question: Explain why saying "a species develops a trait because it needs it" gets the mechanism backwards.
questions.expectedAnswer: Need does not direct mutation toward a requested solution. New variants may arise or arrive, and heritable variants that increase reproductive success can be favored by selection. That reproductive advantage can help cause their spread; chance also matters, and even useful variants are not guaranteed to spread.

history.title: Questions People Ask About Evolution

data.question: Do helpful mutations always spread?
data.answer: No. A trait may help in one setting but not another. Chance can remove a helpful variant before it spreads.

data.question: Does selection explain every evolutionary change?
data.answer: No. Mutation, arriving or leaving genes, and chance also cause change. Genetic drift is change through chance. Its effects are often stronger in small groups.

data.question: Are humans still evolving?
data.answer: Yes. For example, some human populations have inherited traits that let adults keep digesting milk sugar. Evolution concerns inherited changes across generations, and its pace varies.

data.question: What can survival of the fittest leave out?
data.answer: It leaves out reproduction. Fitness concerns the genes passed to later generations compared with others in that setting. It is not a measure of strength or human worth.

data.question: Does adaptation mean perfect design?
data.answer: No. Selection acts on traits that are available. A trait may have costs as well as benefits. A once-useful trait can become less helpful when conditions change.

data.question: Can a neutral variant become common?
data.answer: Yes. Chance can make a variant more common even if it does not help reproduction. This is genetic drift.

data.question: How does antibiotic resistance fit this lesson?
data.answer: Inherited resistance can help microbes leave offspring when a drug is present. New mutations and genes passed between microbes also matter. One survivor does not prove resistance; real cases need more evidence.

data.title: Track the Trait
data.instructions: Model several generations of selection with counters, record how the trait frequency changes, and then audit your own written explanation for the wrong version.
data.fitReason: Counter generations connect inherited variants, reproductive outcomes and measured frequencies. Model limitations prevent a simple color model from being mistaken for complete biology.

brief.context: Use 40 counters or digital tokens in two colors, initially 20 of each. Color represents a heritable variant in a simplified asexual population. The teacher supplies a survival rule that favors one color without deliberately selecting individual counters. After survivors are counted, make 40 offspring by repeatedly sampling one survivor at random with replacement and adding an offspring of that color to a new group. The new group replaces the parents. State that real inheritance can be more complex. No microbes or antibiotics are used.
brief.audience: The class, who will compare frequency graphs and hunt each other's write-ups for the wrong version
brief.drivingQuestion: What exactly is it that changes from one generation to the next?
brief.seedDirection: Record the starting counts before you touch anything. Without generation zero you have nothing to compare against.
lockedLessonFacts: Variation is present at the start of this model; real populations can gain new variants later.
Inherited differences can support evolution when reproductive outcomes differ.
This model fixes the offspring total at 40; overcrowding is not a universal requirement.
Track proportions across generations; individuals also change during life in ways this model omits.
openQuestions: How many generations before the change was obvious?
Did the disfavoured variant disappear completely, and does that matter?
What happened when the environment rule reversed?
stakeholders: Your partner, who is checking your counts
The class, who will read your explanation critically
A student next year who will read the wrong version somewhere and need this
criteria: Starting frequencies recorded before generation one
At least six generations, with counts for each
A graph of the trait frequency across generations
An explanation identifies inheritance, survival, reproduction and frequency; it does not invoke a requested mutation
One sentence saying what your model does not represent well
constraints: State the teacher-supplied survival rule before starting; record any later rule change
Report every generation, including any that went against the trend
Under one page of writing, plus your table and graph
Use counters only. Do not imply that need directs useful mutations or that organisms never grow or learn.
brief.deliverable: A one-page report with your table, your frequency graph, an explanation that survives the language audit, and one sentence on what the counter model fails to capture.

parallelExample.context: A pair ran six generations and their dark counters went from a quarter of the bag to nearly three quarters.
parallelExample.move: They explained both the survival rule and how they sampled offspring to make the next generation. They reported counts, proportions and any rounds against the trend, and compared the results with a repeat run.
parallelExample.whyItHelps: Naming the mechanism and reporting variation across runs is more informative than using or banning a single word such as adapted.

supports.frameStarter: At generation zero, ____ per cent carried ____. By generation six, ____. This happened because ____.
frameChoices: Model a predator that spots one colour more easily
Model a drug that one variant survives
Model a food source only one variant can reach
Model an environment that reverses partway through
coachPrompts: What did you record before generation one?
Where have you shown inheritance and reproductive differences?
What does keeping counter colors fixed represent, and what real lifetime changes does it omit?
What does the bag of counters fail to represent about a real population?

data.coachHint: Record six generations with counts and proportions. Include offspring formation, uncertainty and one limitation of the model.
